content:
Apple TV has just secured global streaming rights to Australian crime series "Dustfall", marking its second recent departure from an original-content-only strategy.

Apple is beginning to acquire more TV series, deviating from its all-original programming approach.

Since Apple TV's launch in 2019, the platform has consistently rejected the typical streaming service practice of acquiring licensed content, instead prioritising original productions.

Apple has remained remarkably consistent in its original-only strategy. Until recently, the only exceptions were children's programming that complemented its original offerings (such as Peanuts holiday specials) and limited-window additional films.

But this week things changed, as the critically acclaimed comedy "Small Prophets" officially premiered on Apple after the platform secured rights to the British hit this summer.

"Small Prophets" appears to be a shrewd acquisition. Early reviews have called it a "masterpiece" and possibly even "Apple's best series this year".

And today, Apple announced its second acquisition. The Australian crime drama starring Anna Torv, "Dustfall", will join the streaming platform in 2027.

Like "Small Prophets", "Dustfall" was created by an international production company and will first air in designated regions overseas before debuting globally on Apple TV.

It's clear Apple's stance on acquisitions has shifted from its previous position.

While the streaming platform has not abandoned its successful originals-first approach, purchasing high-quality series from around the world to enrich its library does represent a strategic shift.

I'm keen to see whether this trend continues to accelerate.

What are your thoughts on Apple TV acquiring third-party series? Feel free to share in the comments section.

Apple TV costs $14.99 per month, or you can subscribe via the Apple One bundle for savings.
